lead: An emission standard is a pair: a test procedure, which for a car is a fixed speed–time trace driven on rollers, and a limit for each pollutant in g/km (light vehicles) or g/kWh (heavy engines). The trace fixes the distance, speeds, accelerations, idle time and cold start, so two vehicles are compared on the same drive. India has used this system through the Bharat Stage (BS) norms, now BS-VI, for cars, two-wheelers, trucks and off-road engines.
prereq: You need: the bench of emission measurement.

blocks.text: A certification test is a script. A driver or robot follows the speed–time trace on a chassis dynamometer, rollers that load the wheels like the road. The car starts cold, after standing overnight at room temperature, because the first minute before the catalyst lights off gives much of the CO and HC. The exhaust is diluted in a CVS system, bag samples are read on the bench, and the mass of each pollutant over the cycle is divided by the distance.
e = m ÷ d;   b = m ÷ W
blocks.where: e is the distance-specific emission in g/km; m the pollutant mass over the cycle in g; d the cycle distance in km; b the brake-specific emission in g/kWh; W the engine work over the cycle in kWh.

blocks.text: A bench reading in ppm is a concentration, a fraction of the gas. A limit in g/km is a mass per unit distance, and a limit in g/kWh is a mass per unit work. A ppm number cannot be compared with either until it is turned into a mass with the gas volume and density, as the second worked example does.

The table gives the BS-VI limits for passenger cars, which match Euro 6. Heavy engines are tested on an engine dynamometer and limited in g/kWh, for example 0.46 g/kWh NOx and 0.01 g/kWh PM on the transient cycle.

Indian cars are certified on the Modified Indian Driving Cycle (MIDC), built on the European NEDC trace: four urban parts of 195 s with speeds up to 50 km/h, then an extra-urban part of 400 s up to 120 km/h, 1180 s and 11.0 km in all. Before that, small vehicles were tested on the slower Indian Driving Cycle. BS-VI two-wheelers use the Worldwide Motorcycle Test Cycle (WMTC). Europe has replaced the NEDC by the WLTC, with longer, faster and more dynamic phases; the United States uses the FTP-75, which weights a cold start and a hot start. Heavy engines use steady and transient engine cycles, such as the WHSC and WHTC.

The cycle matters because speed, acceleration and idle time decide how hot the flame and the catalyst become. A slow urban cycle with a cold start gives more CO and HC per km; a fast, hard cycle gives more NOx. The same car gives different g/km on different traces, which is why a result is meaningless without the name of its cycle.

India went to BS-IV nationwide in April 2017 and skipped BS-V to reach BS-VI in April 2020. Fuel sulphur fell from 50 ppm to 10 ppm, which the catalysts and filters of BS-VI need. BS-VI added particle limits for diesel cars and on-board diagnostics; its second stage, from April 2023, added real driving emission (RDE) checks with portable equipment on public roads. RDE does not replace the laboratory cycle; it checks that the car stays clean away from the script.

Two other rules are often confused with emission limits. Corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) norms cap the average fuel consumption, and so the CO<sub>2</sub> per km, of all the cars a maker sells; they are not a pollutant limit. The pollution under control (PUC) certificate is a quick in-use check: CO and HC at idle for petrol vehicles and free-acceleration smoke for diesels. It is not a type-approval test.

examples.question: A petrol car is certified over the 11.0 km cycle. Its bags hold 0.66 g of NOx, and the BS-VI limit is 0.06 g/km. Find the result. The maker wants a 20 % margin below the limit: find the target in g/km, the NOx mass allowed per test and how much must be removed.
steps: Result: e = m ÷ d = 0.66 g ÷ 11.0 km = 0.060 g/km, exactly at the limit, so there is no margin.
Reduction needed: 0.66 − 0.528 = 0.132 g per test, that is 20 % of the present NOx.
examples.answer: The car emits 0.060 g/km, exactly at the limit; for a 20 % margin it must emit at most 0.528 g per test, 0.132 g less than now.

examples.question: In a CVS test the diluted exhaust totals 150 m³ at standard conditions. The bag reads 3.0 ppm NOx and the dilution-air bag 0.2 ppm. Take NOx as NO<sub>2</sub>, density 2.05 kg/m³ at standard conditions, and a cycle of 11.0 km. Find the NOx in g/km and compare it with 0.06 g/km. (Use the simple background subtraction.)
steps: Against the limit: 0.078 ÷ 0.06 = 1.30, so the car is 30 % over.
examples.answer: NOx is 0.078 g/km, 30 % above the 0.06 g/km limit: the car fails, although its bag reading is only 3 ppm.

traps: Comparing a result from one cycle with a limit written for another.
Calling g/km a “mass per unit work”: g/km is per unit distance; only g/kWh is per unit work.
Deciding pass or fail from a ppm reading: it must first become a mass with the gas volume and density.
Forgetting the cold start, where much of a cycle’s CO and HC is made.
Treating a PUC certificate as a type-approval result, or CAFE as an emission limit.

quiz.q: What two parts make an emission standard?
quiz.a: A test procedure (a driving cycle or engine cycle) and a limit for each pollutant in g/km or g/kWh.

quiz.q: When did India move to BS-IV nationwide and to BS-VI?
quiz.a: BS-IV in April 2017 and BS-VI in April 2020, skipping BS-V.

quiz.q: Why is a certification test a fixed trace and not a real trip?
quiz.a: A fixed trace with a set cold start, speeds and gear changes is repeatable, so every vehicle is judged on the same drive.

quiz.q: Why does a cold start raise CO and HC in a cycle?
quiz.a: The engine runs rich and wets cold walls, and the catalyst is below light-off, so CO and HC leave unconverted for the first minute.

quiz.q: A bag sample holds 0.45 g of CO over a 9.0 km cycle. Does it pass a 1.0 g/km limit?
quiz.a: 0.45 ÷ 9.0 = 0.050 g/km, far below 1.0 g/km, so it passes.

quiz.q: An engine emits 12 g of NOx over a cycle that produces 20 kWh. Does it meet 0.46 g/kWh?
Why did BS-VI add a particle number limit and real driving checks for diesel cars?
quiz.a: A filter that meets the mass limit can still let through many very small particles, which weigh almost nothing; a number limit controls them. Real driving checks catch engines that are clean on the cycle but not in other conditions.

beyond: Not for the exam. Certification now joins the laboratory cycle with portable on-road tests and in-service conformity checks, and the next stages of standards target brake and tyre particles as well as the exhaust. Engineers calibrate engine, catalyst and filter together, because a change that helps one pollutant can hurt another. Search next for “WLTP”, “real driving emissions” and “Euro 7”.

figure.caption: The NEDC speed trace, on which India’s Modified Indian Driving Cycle for cars is built: four urban parts and one extra-urban part, 11.0 km in 1180 s. The shaded first minute is the cold start, where most of the cycle’s CO and HC come out. The worked example divides the bag mass by these 11.0 km.

spec.aria: Vehicle speed against time from 0 to 1180 seconds. Four identical urban parts reach 15, 32 and 50 kilometres per hour with idle between them; the extra-urban part climbs to 70, 50, 70, 100 and 120 kilometres per hour before stopping. The first 60 seconds are shaded as the cold start.
